title: Common Tax Deductions and Credits
summary: DEDUCTION → CREDIT → REFUNDABLE OR NOT → CLAIM
subtitle: Deduction. Credit. People use them interchangeably all the time. They are not the same thing.

blocks.text: Deduction. Credit.
People use the two words as if they mean the same thing. They don’t, and mixing them up is one of the most common sources of tax confusion in this course.
Here’s the short version. A deduction shrinks the income you are taxed on. A credit shrinks the tax bill itself, after that math is done.
Once that clicks, almost everything else in this lesson gets easier.
Claim what you’re owed, and know which claims will put money back in your pocket.
blocks.detail: When you can tell a deduction from a credit, and a refundable credit from one that isn’t, you stop leaving money on the table.
blocks.extra: Section 04 explains the one line that matters most.

blocks.text: Deductions come first. A deduction is taken off your income before tax is worked out.
Say you earned $60,000 and had a $5,000 deduction. Your taxable income drops to $55,000, and tax is worked out on that smaller number.

A deduction is worth your marginal rate, the shelf idea from the Marginal Tax Rates lesson. It’s worth more to someone on a higher shelf, because it shields income that would have been taxed at a higher rate.
Credits come after. Tax is worked out first, on your full taxable income. Then the credit comes straight off the tax bill.
Most credits in Canada are non-refundable. They can bring your tax bill down to zero, but no lower. A smaller number are refundable, which means you get the money even if you owed no tax at all.
That line between refundable and non-refundable matters a lot, and we’ll come back to it.

items.title: A DEDUCTION
items.text: Comes off your income, before tax is worked out. Worth more to higher earners on a higher shelf. Example: an RRSP contribution.

items.title: A CREDIT
items.text: Comes off your tax bill, after tax is worked out. Its value depends on the credit rate and whether it is refundable. Example: the Basic Personal Amount.

items.title: “A $1,000 deduction and a $1,000 credit save you the same amount of tax.”
items.text: They usually don’t. A $1,000 deduction saves $1,000 times your marginal rate, so more for higher earners and less for lower ones. Most federal credits are worked out at the lowest rate, 14%, so a $1,000 credit amount saves about $140 of federal tax, whatever you earn.

sections.title: The deductions most people actually use

items.title: RRSP contributions.
items.text: The best-known deduction. Money you put into a registered retirement savings plan comes off your taxable income.

items.title: Union and professional dues.
items.text: If your job requires membership dues, they’re usually deductible. Check box 44 of your T4.

items.title: Child care expenses.
items.text: Daycare, day camps and caregivers, generally claimed by the spouse with the lower income.

items.title: Moving expenses.
items.text: If you moved at least 40 kilometres closer to a new job or to full-time school.

items.title: FHSA contributions.
items.text: Money you put into a First Home Savings Account is also deductible, up to $8,000 a year.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE REFUNDABLE VS. NON-REFUNDABLE LINE

This is the most important idea in this lesson, and it comes up again and again in this course. A non-refundable credit can only reduce tax you owe. If your tax bill is already near zero, which is common for lower-income or part-time earners, more non-refundable credits put nothing extra in your pocket. There’s no tax left to reduce. A refundable credit is different: you get it whatever tax you owed. The Canada Workers Benefit and the Canada Training Credit are refundable, and the GST/HST credit is paid to you as a benefit. That is why they matter so much for lower-income households. Before you decide a claim isn’t worth it, check which kind it is. The paperwork is often the same. The payoff is not.

items.title: Basic Personal Amount.
items.text: Automatic, and covered in the paycheque lesson. The first slice of your income is never taxed.

items.title: Canada employment amount.
items.text: A small automatic credit for anyone with job income, meant to offset basic work costs.

items.title: Tuition credit.
items.text: For eligible tuition paid to a recognized school. Unused amounts carry forward, or up to $5,000 can be passed to a spouse, parent or grandparent.

items.title: Charitable donation credit.
items.text: 15% federally on the first $200 you give in a year, and 29% on the rest, with a higher rate for top earners.

items.title: Medical expense credit.
items.text: Eligible costs above 3% of your net income or a set dollar amount, whichever is less, for you, your spouse and dependants.

items.title: First-time home buyers’ amount.
items.text: A $10,000 credit amount, worth up to $1,500 federally, in the year you buy your first home.

blocks.text: This is the everyday list, the ones most Canadians use at some point. The Benefits course lesson Tax Credits People Commonly Miss goes deeper into the ones people forget, like caregiving and medical travel.

items.title: “Claiming more deductions and credits always means a bigger refund.”
items.text: Not always. Deductions and non-refundable credits only help if you have income or tax to offset. Piling up claims beyond what your tax bill can use doesn’t create a refund. The extra goes unused, or in some cases carries forward to a later year.

items.title: I know which of my claims are deductions, and which are credits.
I know whether each credit I’m claiming is refundable or non-refundable.
I’ve checked my T4 for union or professional dues I might be missing.
If I have unused tuition credits, I know whether to carry them forward or transfer them.
I haven’t assumed a bigger pile of claims automatically means a bigger refund.

blocks.text: Farida and the RRSP question
paragraphs: Farida was twenty-four, a year out of college and working her first full-time job at a Winnipeg nonprofit. She had $3,000 saved toward a used car, so she could stop biking to work through prairie winters.

One day at lunch, a coworker told her, with total confidence, that smart people maxed out their RRSP every year. Farida felt a pang of guilt. She had already put $1,000 into an RRSP in February, and now she wondered whether the car money belonged there too.

She opened her banking app and got as far as the transfer screen. Then she stopped. Her coworker had been working for fifteen years and earned far more than she did. Before she moved the money, she wanted to know if the same advice fit her income.

At tax time she asked the volunteer at a free tax clinic. He showed her the shelves. Her income was low enough that she sat on the bottom one, so an RRSP deduction this year would save her little. The same deduction would be worth much more once her pay went up.

Then he told her something that surprised her. She didn’t have to claim the $1,000 she had already put in. She could leave it unclaimed on her return and use the deduction in a future year, when her shelf was higher. The money would keep growing in the RRSP in the meantime.
Farida kept her car money and bought a used hatchback in October. Her $1,000 deduction is waiting for a better year. On the first snowy morning, she drove past the bike rack and smiled.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: YOU CAN CONTRIBUTE NOW AND CLAIM LATER

You don’t have to claim an RRSP deduction in the year you contribute. The contribution and the claim are separate steps, and you can carry an unclaimed contribution forward with no deadline. If you contribute in a low-income year, you can hold the deduction for a year when your income and your shelf are higher. This helps most around a raise, a new job or the end of a parental leave: contribute when you have the cash, and time the deduction for the year it saves the most.

Deductions shrink your income before tax is worked out. Credits shrink your tax bill afterward. A deduction is worth more to higher earners, and a credit’s value often depends on whether it’s refundable. Know which is which for every claim, and remember that piling on claims only helps if you have income or tax left to offset.
Time your claims to the year they save you the most.
blocks.detail: A little planning around your shelf can turn the same contribution into a much bigger tax saving.

Answer guidance: if sorting your claims is hard, that’s normal on a first pass. Go back to the definitions above and work through one claim at a time. If you’re on a low shelf this year, a big RRSP deduction may be worth saving for a higher-earning year.

items.title: Deduction
items.text: An amount taken off your income before tax is worked out.

items.title: Credit
items.text: An amount taken off your tax bill after tax is worked out.

items.title: Refundable credit
items.text: Paid to you even if you owed no tax.

items.title: Non-refundable credit
items.text: Can reduce the tax you owe to zero, but cannot create a refund.

items.title: Taxable income
items.text: Your income after deductions come off. This is what your tax bracket applies to.
